summary: BreakGuard statically finds every client (focal) method that calls a library API and asks an LLM, single-shot, to write one JUnit/TestNG test per focal method; a breaking change (BC) counts as detected if a generated test passes on the pre-update version and fails on the post-update version. Evaluated on 89 Java/Maven breaking updates from BUMP with GPT-4o, Qwen3-Coder-480B and GPT-OSS-120B under three context levels. The best configuration (GPT-4o, class context) detects 27/89 (30.3%); 95.1% of detections are crash-type (missing class/method), not behavioural.

claims.claim: Best configuration detects 30.3% (27/89) of breaking changes.
claims.evidence: Table V and RQ2 text: GPT-4o + Class context detects 27/89; Qwen3-Coder max 20 (22.5%), GPT-OSS max 10 (11.2%). Single generation per focal method at temperature 0; no repeated runs.

claims.claim: Mean cost of roughly $0.90 per detected breaking change.
claims.evidence: Table IX column is headed 'USD/detection' but RQ4 text describes $0.90 as the mean cost per BUMP instance (median $0.088); the abstract's 'per detected breaking change' and the intro's 'median ~$0.09 per breaking-update instance' use different units. Per-detection cost (total cost / 27 detections) is never computed explicitly.

claims.claim: LLM-generated tests mostly detect crash-type, not behavioural, BCs.
claims.evidence: RQ3: 95.1% of detections are runtime errors; only 25 tests (0.7% of detecting tests) use value-based assertions; manual inspection of 80 of 455 non-detecting tests that loaded the broken class (32/80 swallowed exceptions in catch blocks, 11/80 used non-triggering inputs).

claims.claim: Class-level context gives the best detection/cost trade-off.
claims.evidence: GPT-4o rises from 17 (Minimal) to 27 (Class) detections, but Qwen3-Coder is flat at 18-20 across contexts and gains nothing from Class context (§V-D). The claim holds for one of three models.

claims.claim: Client test suites often fail to detect BCs, motivating generated tests.
claims.evidence: Asserted with citations in §I; the dataset was filtered to the 188 BUMP instances whose existing client tests already fail, so the evaluation re-detects BCs the client suite already caught. It shows no case where BreakGuard catches a BC the existing tests miss.

patterns.note: Uses execution (two-phase compile/run across pre/post Docker images) as the oracle, but deliberately has no feedback loop; compile rate tops out at 33.5% (Qwen3, class), and the authors argue a compile-error loop would help.
Cross-repo contract checking for library upgrades: tests derived from client usage of a dependency surface 30% of real BCs at low median cost.
LLM-generated tests used as regression detectors rather than test-first development.
Reports token counts and dollar cost per instance; cost dominated by a few clients with >500 focal methods.

methodology.sample: 89 breaking updates (filtered from 571 BUMP; 188 test-failure instances), 31 client projects, 25 libraries, 5,790 focal methods; JSON (27) and logging (26) libraries dominate.
methodology.baselines: None external. No comparison with existing client tests, japicmp/Clirr static API diff, EvoSuite/Randoop, or an agentic repair loop. Context variants and models compared against each other only.
methodology.variance: One generation per focal method; no repeated runs or CIs (acknowledged in §VIII).
methodology.ablations: Three context levels (Minimal, Method, Class) across three models.
methodology.contamination_controls: None; BUMP library versions predate model cutoffs (GPT-4o Oct 2023), so models may know post-update APIs.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; no venue in comment or journal_ref.
standards.artifacts: Paper states code on GitHub and execution data/logs on Zenodo [46]; no GitHub URL extracted in the text.

biases.detail: Only BUMP instances where the client's own test suite already fails were kept, plus a requirement for direct production call sites (60 removed). The setting where BreakGuard would add value (BCs the client suite misses) is not sampled.
Single stochastic generation per focal method; no seeds or reruns.
Cost metric unit is inconsistent between abstract (per detected BC), table header (USD/detection) and text (per BUMP instance).
No external baseline at all. Crash-type BCs (95% of detections) are the class that static API-diff tools like japicmp target, and no comparison with them is made.
Public OSS libraries and versions likely in training data; not discussed.

coi.affiliations: Concordia University (Raj, Costa) and Université de Montréal (Baudry).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: GPT-4o and GPT-OSS (OpenAI), Qwen3-Coder (Alibaba) used as generators; none authored by the paper's authors. BUMP benchmark has Baudry's group lineage (KTH), a mild self-benchmark link.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding statement found.

verdict_reason: Rare Java-native study with a clean execution oracle and honest negative findings (exception-swallowing, crash-only detection). But it has no external baseline, uses a single run per test, the cost metric is inconsistent, and the dataset only contains BCs the client suites already caught, so the added-value claim is unproven.
applicability: Directly relevant to a Java team whose ingestion spans ≥4 repos with shared libraries (Jackson, SLF4J and Spring are in the dataset). Practical use: on Dependabot/Renovate PRs, generate usage-derived tests per call site, run them pre/post in containers, and treat a pass-then-fail as a contract-break signal. Expect it to catch mostly removed/renamed APIs (run japicmp first; it is cheaper) and to miss behavioural changes such as JSON serialisation semantics, which matter most for content delivery to front ends. Add the compile-error feedback loop the paper skipped, plus a lint rule banning broad try/catch in generated tests. Host-agnostic, because it is a CI-side pipeline rather than an agent-host feature. In spec-driven development, contract specs for shared DTOs would supply the behavioural oracle that this approach lacks.
